Pager volume, manual deployments, and ticket queues have consumed all available engineering time leaving nothing for automation or improvement
The ratio of manual operational toil to engineering project work has exceeded sustainable limits, preventing reliability improvements
explanation: Operational overload occurs when manual operational work (toil) consumes so much of the team's capacity that they cannot invest in automation and reliability improvements.

clues: The domain layer looks like the database schema with getters and setters bolted on
Business rules are scattered across service classes rather than living with the data they operate on
Every entity in the domain package could be replaced by a plain struct without breaking anything
OrderService, CustomerService, and InvoiceService each run 2,000 lines of procedural logic over property-only entities
It looks like DDD (entities, repositories, services) but it's really transaction scripts in disguise
Your domain objects are data structures devoid of behavior, with all business logic extracted into external service layers
explanation: An anemic domain model is an anti-pattern where domain objects contain only data (getters/setters) and no business logic, which is instead placed in separate service classes.

clues: One class in your system has grown to thousands of lines and handles everything
New features always seem to require changes to the same massive file
Code reviews on that file take forever because it touches so many concerns
Your UserManager class handles authentication, profile updates, notifications, billing, and reporting
Surrounding classes are mere data holders while one controller class owns nearly all processing: procedural design in OO clothing
One monolithic class has absorbed so many responsibilities that it has become the center of all logic and is impossible to maintain
explanation: The blob (or god class) antipattern is a single class that has grown to encompass too many responsibilities, violating the single responsibility principle.

clues: You can't deploy one module without deploying another, and vice versa

The user never wrote anything, they only read, yet data appears to move backward in time
Successive requests are load-balanced across replicas with different amounts of lag
Pinning each user's reads to one replica (e.g. by hashing user ID) fixes it
After seeing a newer value, a user's later read returns an older one because successive reads hit replicas at different points
explanation: A monotonic read violation occurs when successive reads by the same user are served by replicas at different replication points, causing data to appear to go back in time.

clues: In checkout, step 3 can't see the address saved in step 2, and step 4 sometimes sees it again
The cart flickers between states as the user adds items over several requests
Within one logged-in visit, neither a user's own writes nor the order of their reads is guaranteed
Each request is routed to an arbitrary replica, and no client token records the last version seen
Read-your-writes and monotonic reads, scoped to one user's interaction, are both missing
No consistency guarantee spans a single client's sequence of operations, so one user's visit sees contradictory data states
explanation: Session consistency failure occurs when a distributed system provides no consistency guarantees within a user's session, causing operations to see inconsistent states.

clues: A downstream consumer computed a negative balance because it saw the withdrawal before the deposit
Events are ordered within each Kafka partition, but the merged stream across partitions is scrambled
An observer reading two shards sees a conversation's answer before its question
Different partitions replicate at different speeds, so readers see later writes before earlier ones
The violated guarantee: if writes happen in some order, anyone reading them sees them in that same order
Readers observe a sequence of writes in an order that never happened, typically because the writes went to different partitions
explanation: A consistent prefix violation occurs when readers observe writes in an order inconsistent with the actual write order, typically due to reading from multiple partitions.

clues: A shopper sees '5 in stock', clicks buy, and gets 'sold out'
Two users looking at the same product at the same moment see different prices
The read succeeded, but returned a value that was overwritten seconds earlier
Reads are served from followers to scale, and followers run a few seconds behind the leader
Not about one user's own writes or going backward: any reader may simply get a not-yet-updated value
A read returns an outdated value because it was served by a replica that hasn't yet applied recent writes
explanation: A stale read occurs when a read operation returns outdated data because it was served by a replica that hasn't yet replicated recent writes from the leader.

clues: A replica that was offline for a day still lacks some keys a week later, even keys nobody has read
Inconsistencies only get fixed when someone happens to read the affected key
Scheduled nodetool repair jobs have failed nightly for a month with no alert
The background Merkle-tree comparison between replicas stopped running, so divergence goes undetected
Hinted handoff covered short outages, but nothing reconciles data missed during longer ones
The background process that compares replicas and copies missing data stopped, so replicas permanently diverge
explanation: Anti-entropy failure occurs when the background process that compares replicas and repairs differences stops working, causing permanent data divergence between nodes.

clues: A quorum read returns the right value, but the same stale replica answers with old data again next time
Coordinator logs show digest mismatches on reads, yet replicas never converge afterward
Frequently read keys should self-heal, but they stay inconsistent across replicas
The coordinator detects the out-of-date replica during a read but never writes the newer value back to it
The on-read correction path is broken, not the background sync
The mechanism that pushes newer values to stale replicas during reads fails, leaving detected inconsistencies uncorrected
explanation: Read repair failure occurs when the mechanism that corrects stale replicas during read operations doesn't work, allowing detected inconsistencies to persist indefinitely.

clues: A node came back after a 2-hour crash and then served stale data for another 6 hours
Neighbor nodes buffered the writes it missed, but replaying them to it is crawling
The replay throttle on the delivery stream is set to 1 MB/s cluster-wide
Millions of buffered entries for the recovered node sit on other nodes, bottlenecked on disk I/O
Writes accepted on the downed node's behalf are delivered too slowly once it recovers
Buffered writes held on behalf of a temporarily down node are replayed too slowly after recovery, prolonging stale reads
explanation: Hinted handoff delay occurs when writes buffered for an unavailable node take too long to be replayed after recovery, keeping the node in an inconsistent state.

clues: Reads return stale data even though W + R > N is configured
During a partial outage, writes kept succeeding with W=2, but reads afterward missed them
Those writes were acknowledged by nodes that don't normally own that key
The database is set to accept writes on any reachable nodes during failures so it stays writable
Overlap between the write and read node sets is only guaranteed among the key's home replicas
When writes can land on any reachable nodes instead of the key's designated replicas, W+R>N no longer guarantees fresh reads
explanation: Sloppy quorum confusion occurs when writes go to nodes outside the designated replica set during partial failures, breaking the consistency guarantee of strict quorums.

clues: Disk usage keeps growing even though the app deletes as many rows as it inserts
Range scans over a queue-like table got 100x slower, though few rows are live

Deletes write markers instead of removing data, and compaction hasn't purged them past gc_grace_seconds
Every deleted entry leaves behind a marker that each read must skip over
Deletion markers in an LSM-tree pile up because compaction isn't purging them, bloating storage and slowing reads
explanation: Tombstone accumulation occurs when deletion markers in LSM-trees or similar structures are not cleaned up by compaction, bloating storage and degrading read performance.

clues: Write throughput is fine, but read latency rises a little more every day
Disk usage grows faster than the live data set
Each read now consults 40 sorted files instead of the usual 4
Cassandra's pending-tasks metric for background merges climbs steadily and never drains
The LSM tree's background merge process can't keep up with the incoming write rate
Background merging of sorted files falls behind write throughput, so reads touch ever more files
explanation: Compaction lag occurs when the background compaction process in an LSM-tree storage engine cannot keep up with the write rate, degrading read performance over time.

clues: A table with 10GB of live data occupies 120GB on disk
Most on-disk files hold superseded versions of keys overwritten long ago
The write rate is modest and steady, so the merge process isn't overloaded, yet the file count keeps rising
Someone disabled automatic merging on the LevelDB store during a migration and never re-enabled it
The number of sorted string table files and their key-range overlap has exploded, multiplying read I/O
Too many overlapping immutable sorted files pile up from misconfigured or disabled compaction, wasting disk and amplifying reads
explanation: SSTable bloat occurs when too many overlapping SSTable files accumulate because compaction is misconfigured or disabled, wasting storage on superseded data and causing excessive read amplification.

clues: Switching primary keys from auto-increment to random UUIDv4 doubled insert latency
p99 insert latency shows sharp outliers while the median stays flat

Inserting into a full B-tree node forces it to split in two and update its parent, causing write latency and I/O spikes
explanation: B-tree page split overhead causes write latency spikes and index bloat when inserts land in full nodes, forcing them to split into two half-full pages and update parent pointers; random keys like UUIDv4 make splits far more frequent than sequential keys.

clues: Exact-key lookups take microseconds, but WHERE created_at BETWEEN ... does a full scan despite an index
EXPLAIN shows the index ignored for ORDER BY and LIKE 'abc%' queries

Index lookups are O(1), but there's no way to iterate keys in sorted order
The index places keys using a function that deliberately destroys their ordering
A hash-based index gives fast point lookups but can't serve range scans or ordered iteration, and its keys must fit in memory
explanation: Hash indexes provide fast point lookups but cannot support range queries or ordered scans, since hashing destroys key ordering; in-memory hash indexes like Bitcask's also require all keys to fit in RAM.

clues: Lookups for keys that don't exist are as slow as lookups for keys that do
Disk read IOPS spike whenever a client probes for missing keys
Per-file filters are configured at 2 bits per key, giving roughly a 40% false positive rate

Raising bits_per_key from 2 to 10 dropped false positives to about 1%
A probabilistic set filter sized with too few bits per key returns too many false positives, defeating its purpose of avoiding disk reads
explanation: Bloom filter misconfiguration occurs when the filter's parameters are set incorrectly, causing excessive false positives that defeat its purpose of reducing unnecessary disk reads.

clues: One node of a six-node cluster takes nearly all writes, and which node it is changes every hour
Adding nodes didn't increase write throughput at all
Historical queries spread nicely, but all current inserts land on a single partition
IoT sensor events use a key prefixed by the current hour, so they range-partition to the same node
Prefixing keys with the sensor ID before the time spreads the load
Partitioning time-ordered data by timestamp concentrates all current writes on one partition
explanation: A time-series data hotspot occurs when timestamp-based partitioning concentrates all current writes on a single partition, defeating the purpose of distributed storage.

clues: 'All orders from January to March' takes 30x longer than fetching one order by ID
Traces show a date-range query fanning out to all 64 partitions
After migrating to a distributed database, point lookups got faster but ordered scans got far slower
Order IDs are spread across nodes by a function that balances load but randomizes key placement
Adjacent keys end up on different partitions, so any range needs scatter-gather
Data partitioned by a hash of the key can't serve range queries efficiently because adjacent keys are scattered everywhere
explanation: Range queries on hash-partitioned data require scatter-gather across all partitions because hash functions destroy key ordering, spreading adjacent keys across the cluster.

clues: Data is evenly spread across partitions, yet one partition gets 90% of requests

A small number of keys receive a disproportionate share of traffic
Request load is concentrated on a few very popular keys, creating hot partitions that even data distribution can't fix
explanation: A skewed workload occurs when certain keys receive disproportionately more traffic than others, creating hot partitions that no partitioning strategy can fully prevent.

clues: Looking up a user by email is 20x slower than looking up by user ID

Adding an index on 'color' didn't avoid fan-out: finding all red cars still queries every partition

Per-partition indexes on a non-key field force querying all partitions, since each indexes only its own data
explanation: Secondary index scatter occurs with document-partitioned indexes where queries on indexed fields must fan out to all partitions, as each partition only indexes its own documents.

clues: A product listing saves successfully but doesn't show up in search for several seconds
Reading by primary key returns the new item immediately, but querying by category doesn't

The managed key-value store documents that queries on non-key attributes are only eventually consistent

explanation: Global secondary index lag occurs when a term-partitioned index is updated asynchronously, causing a delay between data writes and the data appearing in index-based queries.

clues: Transfers between accounts on the same shard take 5 ms; transfers across shards take 200 ms
Timeouts spike only for operations touching more than one shard

Transactions spanning several partitions need distributed coordination like 2PC, adding latency and reducing availability
explanation: Cross-partition transactions require distributed coordination protocols that dramatically increase latency and reduce availability compared to single-partition operations.

clues: A customer was charged, but their order never shipped and no refund was issued

A long-running business process built from local transactions plus undo steps left partial side effects
Compensating transactions in a multi-service sequence of local transactions fail to run after a step fails, leaving permanent inconsistency
explanation: Saga coordination failure occurs when a distributed saga fails to execute compensating transactions after a step fails, leaving the system in a permanently inconsistent state.

clues: Billing shows duplicate charges after a consumer pod restarted

The false belief that messages can be delivered exactly once; in reality it's at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing
explanation: The exactly-once delivery myth is the false assumption that message brokers can guarantee exactly-once delivery; in practice, at-least-once with idempotent consumers is required.

clues: A payment request timed out, the client retried, and the customer was charged twice

explanation: Idempotency key absence is the lack of a client-supplied unique key on API requests that allows the server to detect and deduplicate retried operations.

clues: Latency spikes every weekday around 2 p.m., though our own traffic is flat

explanation: Noisy Neighbor occurs when a co-tenant on shared infrastructure monopolizes resources, causing performance degradation for other tenants.

clues: Calls to the geocoding API start failing around the 27th of each month and recover on the 1st

explanation: Quota Exhaustion happens when a service exceeds its allocated usage limits, causing requests to be rejected until the quota resets.

clues: During a flash sale, the API went from healthy to unresponsive within seconds

explanation: Rate Limiting Absence means a system has no controls to restrict the volume of requests from individual clients, making it vulnerable to overload.

clues: The service runs fine for an hour under sustained load, then dies with OutOfMemoryError

explanation: Backpressure Failure occurs when a system lacks flow control mechanisms, allowing producers to overwhelm consumers with more work than they can process.

clues: End-to-end latency grows by minutes every hour while per-message processing time stays constant

Consumers run at normal speed, but enqueue rate exceeded dequeue rate long enough that the backlog never recovered
Messages pile up in the queue faster than they are consumed, driving unbounded latency and resource use
explanation: Queue Depth Explosion happens when messages accumulate in a queue faster than they can be consumed, causing growing latency and resource exhaustion.

clues: Requests time out, yet the database shows low CPU and few active queries
Logs show 'Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms'

Raising maxPoolSize from 10 to 50 helps briefly, then the problem returns at higher load
A few slow reporting queries hold their connections for minutes, starving everyone else
Every connection in the app's pool is checked out, so new requests block waiting for one to be returned
explanation: Connection Pool Exhaustion occurs when all connections in a pool are in use, causing new requests to block or fail while waiting for an available connection.

clues: The service stops responding, but CPU is at 3% and memory is normal

A dependency got slow, and calls without timeouts held every worker hostage
In .NET, calling .Result on async tasks inside request handlers is a classic trigger
Every worker in the pool is blocked on slow operations, leaving none to pick up new tasks
explanation: Thread Pool Starvation happens when all threads in a pool are occupied by long-running or blocked operations, preventing new work from being processed.

clues: The service must be restarted every four days or it becomes unresponsive

GC can't free objects that are still referenced, even if they'll never be used again
Objects are retained after they're no longer needed, so memory grows until the process is killed
explanation: A Memory Leak in Production is the gradual accumulation of unreleased memory allocations that eventually exhausts available heap and crashes the process.

clues: p99 latency spikes in 100 ms bursts while the host's CPU sits at 40%

explanation: CPU Throttling occurs when a container's process is paused by the kernel scheduler after exceeding its allocated CPU time quota within a scheduling period.

clues: Queries that usually take 2 ms take 2 s with identical plans

iostat shows %util at 100% and an average queue size over 50 on the data volume

Burst credits on the cloud block volume ran out, dropping it to baseline IOPS
The storage device has hit its throughput or IOPS ceiling, so every read and write queues behind others
explanation: Disk I/O Saturation occurs when a storage device reaches its maximum throughput or IOPS capacity, causing all read and write operations to queue.

clues: Users in us-east can use the app while users in eu-west get errors, with nothing deployed

How a distributed system behaves when nodes can't communicate: refuse requests to stay consistent, or keep serving and risk divergence
explanation: Network Partition Handling refers to how a distributed system behaves when network failures prevent nodes from communicating, as described by the CAP theorem.

clues: All outbound calls from one cluster failed at once, while calls to hardcoded IPs kept working

CoreDNS pods were OOMKilled and stopped answering queries
Name-to-IP translation fails because the configured resolver is unreachable or returning errors
explanation: DNS Resolution Failure occurs when the DNS resolver is unavailable or misconfigured, preventing hostname-to-IP translation for all network requests.

clues: At exactly 00:00 UTC every client started failing to connect to our API, with no deploy

explanation: TLS Certificate Expiry occurs when an SSL/TLS certificate passes its not-after date, causing clients to reject connections as untrusted.

clues: JWTs issued by one service are rejected by another as 'not yet valid (nbf)'

chronyc tracking shows one host is 47 seconds off from the others

explanation: Clock Skew is the difference in system time between machines in a distributed system, which can cause failures in time-dependent protocols and ordering.

clues: A server ran out of disk overnight and the app crashed with ENOSPC
du shows /var/log/app/app.log at 200GB, a single file

Old log files aren't being rotated, compressed and purged, so logs grow until they fill the disk
explanation: Log Rotation Failure occurs when the automated process to archive and purge old log files stops working, causing logs to consume all available disk space.

clues: New processes fail with 'fork: Resource temporarily unavailable', yet CPU and memory are low

clues: A critical process vanished with no application error logs and no stack trace

clues: A production host became completely unresponsive: no SSH, no ping, nothing in the app logs

explanation: A kernel panic is a fatal, unrecoverable error inside the OS kernel that halts the entire machine; recovery depends on auto-reboot settings, watchdog timers, and redundancy.

clues: One runaway pod consumed all memory on a node, and unrelated pods were evicted

explanation: Container Resource Limits define CPU and memory boundaries for containers, enabling proper scheduling and preventing resource monopolization.

clues: Dozens of pods across the cluster terminated within minutes, though nothing was deployed

kubelet events show 'The node was low on resource: memory'

explanation: A Pod Eviction Storm occurs when resource pressure causes Kubernetes to evict pods across multiple nodes in a cascading chain reaction.

clues: Autoscaling is configured, but every morning traffic ramp still causes 5 minutes of errors

clues: A deployment has been stuck at 5 of 10 new replicas for an hour

clues: Right after switching the router to the new environment, users see data inconsistencies

clues: Nobody can say which features break when the profile service goes down

clues: One team's unindexed report query slows checkout for three other services

clues: A backend deploy broke three mobile app versions still in users' hands

clues: The provider's change passed all of its own tests but broke two consumers
Consumer teams published their expectations as Pact files, but the provider never ran them
Removing an 'optional' field broke consumers whose recorded expectations required it
Running the consumer-written suite against the new provider build would have failed
The broker's can-i-deploy check marks the provider version incompatible with the payments consumer
A provider change breaks expectations its consumers defined and published, which the provider was obligated to verify
explanation: A Consumer-Driven Contract Violation occurs when a provider changes its service in ways that break the contracts defined by its consumers.

clues: The legacy migration started two years ago, and the old system still handles 70% of traffic
New features are being built in both the old and new systems
The routing proxy that decides old vs. new per endpoint has become its own unmaintainable mess
Management moved the migration team to feature work, and the legacy system keeps growing
Incremental, route-by-route replacement stalled midway, leaving two systems to maintain
A gradual replacement, where new code grows around the legacy system until it can be cut away, stalled halfway
explanation: A Strangler Fig Pattern Stall occurs when the incremental migration from a legacy system loses momentum, leaving the organization stuck maintaining both systems.

clues: Two implementations of the payment engine coexist in trunk, and neither is fully trusted
The interface introduced to swap components exposes details of the old one
The new implementation can't fit the interface, which was shaped around the old one's quirks
A runtime toggle routing between old and new code paths has stayed in place for 18 months
Teams gave up on the in-trunk, incremental component swap and now maintain both paths
A seam added in mainline to incrementally swap a component failed because it didn't properly encapsulate both implementations
explanation: Branch by Abstraction Failure occurs when the abstraction layer meant to enable incremental component replacement is too leaky or poorly designed to work.

clues: QA says the configuration space is untestable: there are 2^200 possible combinations
Nobody knows which runtime switches are still active or who owns them
The code is littered with if (isEnabled('new_checkout_v2')) checks, some nested three deep
Switches added for releases three years ago remain because nobody is confident removing them
The flag dashboard lists 600 entries, and 400 haven't changed state in a year
Hundreds of feature flags accumulated and were never retired, creating an unmanageable test matrix and code complexity
explanation: Feature Toggle Explosion is the accumulation of too many feature flags that are never retired, creating unmaintainable complexity.

clues: Every release needs a two-week stabilization phase to merge long-lived branches
Feature branches commonly live for three months
Engineers object 'we'll break main' when asked to integrate daily
Proposals to hide unfinished work behind flags were rejected in architecture review
The team refuses short-lived branches and committing to the mainline at least once a day
The team rejects having everyone integrate small changes into one shared main branch often, preferring long-lived branches
explanation: Trunk-Based Development Resistance is a team's refusal to commit to the main branch frequently, preferring long-lived branches that cause integration pain.

clues: The week before each release is consumed by fixing things that worked in isolation
Every feature works on its own branch but fails once combined
'Merge day' means late nights debugging emergent issues across modules
The bugs come from conflicting assumptions between teams, not just textual conflicts
Code is combined only at the end of the cycle, so every incompatibility surfaces at once
Infrequent integration makes the end-of-cycle merge-and-stabilize phase agonizing; continuous integration was invented to prevent it
explanation: Integration Hell is the painful period that results from infrequent integration, where merging long-diverged branches creates cascading conflicts and bugs.

clues: A merge has been in progress for three days, and new conflicts keep appearing
Resolving conflicts in one file creates new ones in files already resolved
A big rename refactor on main restructured files the feature branch had heavily edited
While we resolve, main keeps moving, so the branch falls further behind
The longer we wait, the worse it gets, so we wait even longer
Conflict resolution creates more divergence, which creates more conflicts, a self-reinforcing loop that makes merging ever harder
explanation: A Merge Conflict Spiral occurs when resolving merge conflicts creates new conflicts, making the merge progressively more difficult.

clues: Our branching strategy has become so complex that developers spend more time managing branches than writing code.
We have develop, release, hotfix, feature, and support branches, each with their own rules and merge targets.
Cherry-picking commits between branches has led to duplicate commits and inconsistent history.
New developers take weeks to understand when to branch from where and merge into what.
The branching model that was designed for structure has become a source of overhead and errors.
The team's Git branching strategy is overly complex, with too many long-lived branches and merge paths that create confusion and overhead.
explanation: A Git Workflow Antipattern is an overly complex branching strategy that creates more overhead and confusion than the structure it was meant to provide.

clues: Median time from PR open to first review is 3 days
Developers start new work while waiting and have forgotten the details when feedback arrives
Two senior engineers must approve everything, and they're also on call
Developers batch changes into huge PRs because each wait is long, making reviews even slower
DORA metrics show lead time dominated by waiting for approval, not coding or CI
Too few reviewers can't keep up with incoming PRs, so changes queue and throughput drops
explanation: A Code Review Bottleneck occurs when the review process becomes a chokepoint, with too few reviewers causing PRs to queue for days.

clues: The CI suite takes four hours, so engineers push before leaving and read the results the next morning.
Most of our tests spin up browsers and databases, making them slow and prone to environmental issues.
We have very few unit tests but hundreds of end-to-end tests that cover the same logic.
Test failures are often due to timing issues, browser quirks, or test environment instability rather than actual bugs.
The team wrote high-level integration tests first and never backfilled the fast, isolated unit tests.
The testing strategy has too many slow, brittle end-to-end tests and too few fast unit tests, inverting the ideal test distribution pyramid.
explanation: Test Pyramid Inversion occurs when a test suite has more slow, high-level tests than fast, low-level tests, inverting the recommended distribution.

clues: Our QA team spends most of their time clicking through the application manually to verify changes.
Automated tests are few and mostly GUI-level, while manual testing constitutes the bulk of quality assurance.
The test strategy is top-heavy: mostly manual and UI tests, with almost no unit or integration tests.
Regression testing takes a full week because it's all done manually by the QA team.
When visualized, the test distribution looks like an upside-down pyramid with manual testing on top.
The testing strategy relies primarily on manual testing at the top, with automated GUI tests below, and almost no unit tests at the base, forming an ice cream cone shape.
explanation: Ice Cream Cone Testing is an antipattern where the testing strategy is dominated by manual and UI tests with minimal automated unit testing.

clues: Developers routinely re-run the CI pipeline two or three times before a green build, treating failures as noise.
The same test passes and fails on identical code without any changes between runs.
The team has lost confidence in the test suite and frequently ignores test failures.
Race conditions, shared state, and time-dependent assertions cause unpredictable test outcomes.
Over 15% of test runs produce at least one spurious failure, leading to a 'just retry it' culture.
A large proportion of tests fail intermittently and nondeterministically, eroding team confidence in the entire test suite.
explanation: A Flaky Test Epidemic is when a significant portion of tests fail intermittently, causing the team to lose trust in the test suite and ignore real failures.

clues: Tests pass locally but fail in CI because they depend on specific data being present in a shared database.
A test asserting 'customer #4512 has 3 orders' broke after someone placed a manual test order on that account.
The test database has accumulated years of manually inserted data that nobody understands or documents.
A developer truncated a table to fix their test, breaking 30 other tests that depended on that data.
There are no factories or fixtures; tests rely on rows a QA engineer hand-inserted into the shared test DB years ago.
Tests have no strategy for creating, isolating, and cleaning up their own data, relying on a shared, hand-curated database.
explanation: Test Data Management Failure is the absence of a strategy for test data lifecycle, causing tests to depend on shared mutable state.

clues: Unit tests pass with 95% coverage, yet the app breaks the first time the real components are wired together.
A reviewer notes the OrderService test has 14 lines of when(...).thenReturn(...) setup and two lines exercising real code.
Even pure helpers and value objects like Money and DateRange are replaced with fakes in the tests.
A null returned by the real repository went unnoticed because the stubbed repository in tests never returns null.
The tests only prove the code calls its fakes the way the author imagined, not that real collaborators behave that way.
Tests replace nearly every real dependency with mocks, so they verify interactions between fakes and give false confidence.
explanation: Mocking Overuse is when tests replace too many real dependencies with mocks, testing only interaction patterns rather than actual behavior.

clues: Reordering test execution causes some tests to fail that previously passed.
A test that verifies user creation fails when run after a test that clears the users table.
We cannot run a subset of the test suite because tests depend on side effects from previous tests.
Parallelizing tests causes widespread failures because tests implicitly share state.
testLogin only passes if testRegisterUser ran first in the same process, because it reuses the user that test created.
Tests depend on shared mutable state or the execution order of other tests, making them impossible to run in isolation or in parallel.
explanation: Test Coupling occurs when tests depend on each other through shared state or execution order, preventing independent and parallel execution.

clues: We have a CI server running but developers rarely look at its results or fix broken builds promptly.
The build has been red for three weeks and the team continues to merge code on top of it.
Failed tests are routinely skipped or marked as 'known failures' to keep the pipeline green.
The CI pipeline exists but doesn't actually prevent broken code from reaching the main branch.
Management reports 'we do CI' but the practice provides no actual feedback loop or quality gate.
The team has CI tooling in place but doesn't follow CI practices like fixing broken builds immediately, making the CI server purely ceremonial.
explanation: Continuous Integration Theater is having CI infrastructure without the discipline of keeping builds green and acting on failures promptly.

clues: Deploying a one-line change to a single service requires a coordinated deployment of the entire platform.
Our deploy script builds and ships all 40 service repos together, tagged with a single platform version number.
If any single component in the release fails validation, the entire release is rolled back.
A billing hotfix had to wait while the search team fixed an unrelated failing test in their own service.
The deployment pipeline treats all services as a single deployable unit despite them being separate codebases.
All services must be deployed together as a single unit, preventing teams from releasing changes independently despite having separate codebases.
explanation: A Deployment Monolith is when independently developed services are forced into a single deployment unit, preventing independent release cycles.

clues: The production database schema doesn't match what the migration scripts produce on a fresh database.
Someone applied a manual ALTER TABLE in production months ago that was never captured in a migration file.
Different environments have slightly different schemas because migrations were applied inconsistently.
A new developer's local database has a different schema than staging, causing bugs that only appear in production.
There is no single source of truth for the database schema because ad-hoc changes bypass the migration process.
The database schema has diverged from what the migration scripts define because manual changes were made directly to production without corresponding migration files.
explanation: Database Migration Drift occurs when the actual database schema diverges from the migration-defined schema due to untracked manual changes.

clues: Adding a column to one service's database table requires changes in three other services.
Services directly query each other's database tables rather than communicating through APIs.
A database index change in the orders service broke the reporting service's queries.
Teams cannot independently evolve their data models because other teams depend on their table structures.
The shared schema acts as a hidden contract that tightly binds services at the data layer.
Multiple services are coupled through direct dependencies on each other's database schemas, making any schema change a cross-team coordination effort.
explanation: Schema Coupling occurs when services depend directly on each other's database schemas, creating tight coupling at the data layer.

clues: Simple CRUD operations that used to take an hour now take a full sprint to implement.
Debugging production issues requires replaying thousands of events to reconstruct the current state.
Event schema evolution has become a nightmare because old events must remain parseable forever.
The team needs to maintain event upcasters for dozens of versions of the same event type.
What was intended to provide a complete audit trail has become an unmanageable source of operational complexity.
Adopting event sourcing for the entire system has made simple operations incredibly complex, with event versioning, replay, and projection maintenance consuming most development effort.
explanation: Event Sourcing Complexity Explosion occurs when the overhead of maintaining event stores, projections, and schema evolution outweighs the benefits.

clues: A critical production server went down and we cannot rebuild it because nobody remembers how it was configured.
This server has been running for years and has accumulated dozens of manual tweaks and patches.
The configuration on this machine differs from every other machine in the fleet in subtle, undocumented ways.
It was set up by an engineer who left the company, and the only documentation is tribal knowledge.
The box is named legacy-prod-01, has 1,400 days of uptime, and everyone is afraid to reboot it.
A server that has been manually configured over time into a unique state that cannot be reproduced from automation or documentation.
explanation: A Snowflake Server is a manually configured server whose unique state cannot be reliably reproduced, making it irreplaceable and fragile.

clues: Deploying the same code to a new environment requires searching through code to change hardcoded values.
Database credentials are scattered across multiple configuration files with no central management.
Different team members have different configuration file formats that serve the same purpose.
The application reads some config from files, some from environment variables, and some from command-line args inconsistently.
There is no single, consistent approach to how the application consumes its runtime configuration.
The application's configuration is managed inconsistently, with values hardcoded, scattered across files, and mixed with code rather than being cleanly separated.
explanation: Configuration Management Antipattern is the inconsistent handling of application configuration, violating the principle of strict separation of config from code.

clues: After deploying, an engineer SSHed into production to apply a quick fix that was never captured in the deployment pipeline.
The running servers have diverged from what the deployment pipeline would produce if re-run.
We cannot confidently recreate our production environment because manual patches have been applied in place.
A security audit found that production servers have packages installed that aren't in the official build.
The pattern of modifying running servers instead of rebuilding from a known definition has created configuration drift.
Running infrastructure is being modified in place rather than being replaced with new instances built from immutable, versioned artifacts.
explanation: Immutable Infrastructure Violation occurs when running servers are patched in place rather than replaced from versioned build artifacts.

clues: Deployments take 15 minutes because pulling the container image over the network is extremely slow.
The container image is 4GB even though the application itself is only 50MB of compiled code.
Build tools, debug utilities, and source code are all included in the production image.
The Dockerfile starts FROM ubuntu:latest and installs a full development toolchain for the build step.
Using a multi-stage build reduces the image size from 4GB to 150MB.
The production container image includes unnecessary build dependencies, development tools, and intermediate artifacts, making it excessively large.
explanation: Container Image Bloat occurs when production images include unnecessary build tools, dependencies, and artifacts, increasing size and attack surface.

clues: A customer reported seeing another customer's data in their dashboard after a recent deployment.
Configuration values for tenant isolation are loaded at startup and cached without tenant context.
A tenant-specific database connection string was accidentally shared across tenant boundaries.
The environment variable for the database URL doesn't include tenant identification, pointing all tenants to the same store.
Tenant configuration was not properly scoped, causing one tenant's settings to bleed into another's requests.
Configuration meant for one tenant is being applied to requests from a different tenant due to improper scoping of tenant-specific settings.
explanation: Multi-Tenancy Configuration Leak is when tenant-specific configuration is not properly isolated, allowing one tenant's settings to affect another.

clues: Our configuration system has hundreds of entries, most of which no one can explain the purpose of.
Turning off an old flag caused an outage because production code still referenced it in an unexpected code path.
New engineers are afraid to clean up old flags because there's no documentation of what depends on them.
The feature flag evaluation logic adds measurable latency because it checks hundreds of conditions per request.
Flags that were meant to last one sprint have been in production for two years with no owner or expiration date.
Accumulated feature flags that were never retired have become a liability, with unknown dependencies and no documentation of their intended lifecycle.
explanation: Feature Flag Configuration Debt is the accumulation of stale, undocumented feature flags that become a maintenance burden and source of risk.

clues: Users experience inconsistent behavior because they're enrolled in conflicting experiments.
The A/B testing system has 300 active experiments, and nobody knows which ones are still being analyzed.
Experiments interact with each other in unexpected ways, contaminating statistical results.
The configuration for experiments is spread across a database, a config file, and a third-party service.
Cleaning up concluded experiments is nobody's responsibility, so they accumulate indefinitely.
A/B test configurations have proliferated without governance, creating hundreds of active experiments that interact unpredictably and are never cleaned up.
explanation: A/B Test Configuration Sprawl is the uncontrolled growth of experiment configurations that interact unpredictably and lack lifecycle management.

clues: Our staging branch and production branch have diverged so much that cherry-picks frequently fail.
Each environment has its own long-lived branch with environment-specific changes committed directly to it.
Promoting code from dev to staging to production involves complex merge operations between branches.
Configuration that should differ per environment is baked into the code on each branch.
We maintain separate Git branches for dev, staging, and production instead of using environment variables for differences.
The team maintains separate long-lived Git branches per environment, mixing code changes with environment-specific configuration directly in the branch.
explanation: Per-Environment Branching is the antipattern of maintaining separate Git branches for each deployment environment instead of using external configuration.

clues: A security scan flagged our repository for containing sensitive credentials in committed files.
An engineer discovered our production database password in a configuration file checked into Git.
Rotating the compromised credential requires a code change, review, and deployment rather than an environment variable update.
The secret has been in the Git history for months, meaning anyone with repository access has had access to production.
Even though we deleted the file, the secret is still accessible in the Git commit history.
Sensitive infrastructure credentials like database passwords and API keys have been committed directly into the source code repository.
explanation: Infrastructure Secret in Code is the dangerous practice of committing sensitive credentials directly into version control rather than managing them externally.

clues: Moving the application to a new database server requires a code change and redeployment.
The database connection string is defined as a constant in the application's source code.
We accidentally connected our staging application to the production database because someone forgot to change the hardcoded URL.
Developers each have different local database URLs, so they keep uncommitted changes to the config file.
The connection string should be injected as an environment variable so the same code can connect to any database instance.
The database connection URL is hardcoded in source code rather than being provided as an environment variable, preventing the same build from running against different databases.
explanation: Database URL Hardcoding is embedding database connection strings directly in code instead of treating them as external configuration.

clues: Switching our payment processor requires rewriting half the codebase because payment logic is deeply embedded everywhere.
The vendor's SDK types are used directly in our domain model and API responses.
When the vendor's API was down for an hour, our entire application became nonfunctional.
There is no abstraction layer between our business logic and the external service's API.
Stripe's Charge object is persisted as-is in our orders table and returned verbatim from our public API.
The application is directly coupled to a third-party service's API throughout the codebase, making it impossible to swap providers without extensive rewrites.
explanation: Third-Party Service Tight Coupling occurs when an application integrates directly with an external service API without an abstraction layer, violating backing service portability.

clues: Our application directly opens SMTP connections to send email, tightly binding it to a specific mail server.
Switching from SendGrid to Mailgun requires changes in 30 different files across the application.
Email sending is synchronous in the request path, causing timeouts when the mail server is slow.
The SMTP server's hostname and credentials are used directly in business logic code, not injected as a backing service.
Email should be treated as an attached resource that can be swapped by changing a URL, not rewiring application code.
The application integrates directly with a specific email provider's API throughout the codebase instead of treating email as a swappable attached resource.
explanation: Email Service Direct Integration violates the twelve-factor principle of treating backing services as attached resources by hardcoding a specific email provider.

clues: Our application uses Redis-specific commands throughout the codebase, making it impossible to use any other cache.
When the Redis cluster had an outage, caching failures cascaded through the entire application because there was no fallback.
Switching to Memcached would require rewriting every caching call because Redis-specific data structures are used everywhere.
The caching layer has no abstraction; Lua scripts and sorted sets are called directly from business logic.
The cache should be an attached resource swappable via URL, but our code is deeply tied to one implementation.
The application is tightly coupled to a specific caching technology's APIs and data structures, preventing it from being swapped as an attached resource.
explanation: Cache Service Tight Coupling is when application code depends directly on a specific cache implementation rather than treating the cache as a swappable backing service.

clues: Migrating from AWS SQS to RabbitMQ would require changes to every message producer and consumer.
Our message publishing code directly uses vendor-specific SDK classes and features like SQS FIFO deduplication.
Developers can't run the app offline because every local test hits a real SQS queue in a shared AWS account.
Business logic is intertwined with queue-specific acknowledgment patterns and visibility timeout extensions.
The message queue should be a backing service attachable via URL, but vendor-specific features are used throughout.
The application is locked into a specific message queue vendor because vendor-specific APIs and features are used directly throughout the codebase.
explanation: Queue Service Vendor Lock-In occurs when an application uses vendor-specific queue features directly, preventing it from treating the queue as a swappable attached resource.

clues: Our production deployment sometimes fails because npm install pulls a different version of a dependency.
The deploy process compiles code on the production server, occasionally failing due to missing build tools.
Two deployments of the same commit produced different artifacts because dependencies changed between them.
We should build once, produce an immutable artifact, then deploy that same artifact to every environment.
The twelve-factor methodology requires strict separation between the build, release, and run stages.
The deployment process includes a compilation or build step rather than deploying a pre-built immutable artifact, violating build-release-run separation.
explanation: Build Step in Deployment violates the twelve-factor build/release/run separation by compiling code during deployment rather than deploying pre-built artifacts.

clues: A deployment introduced a critical bug and it took four hours to recover because we had no way to revert.
The team had to frantically fix-forward because the previous version's artifacts were not preserved.
Database migrations in the release were not backward-compatible, so reverting the code would break the schema.
There is no release versioning system; each deploy overwrites the previous state completely.
The twelve-factor app mandates that releases are append-only with the ability to roll back to any previous release.
Releases are not versioned or preserved, and deployments include irreversible changes, making it impossible to quickly revert to a known-good state.
explanation: Release Without Rollback Plan is deploying without preserving previous release artifacts or ensuring backward compatibility, making quick recovery impossible.

clues: A nightly report scheduled with an in-process setInterval silently didn't run because a deploy restarted the app at 1:59am.
Background jobs held in an in-memory queue vanish whenever the container is recycled.
After a database failover the app never reconnects; it stays broken until someone restarts it by hand.
Ops only deploys at night because a restart means a 20-minute warm-up and lost in-flight work.
The design assumes the process stays up for months, but the platform recycles containers daily.
The app is built as if its process is permanent, keeping jobs, timers and state in memory instead of treating processes as disposable.
explanation: Long-Running Process Assumption is designing an application that expects to run indefinitely rather than treating processes as ephemeral and disposable.

clues: Users occasionally see 502 errors during deployments even though we use rolling updates.
In-flight HTTP requests are terminated abruptly when old pods are killed during a rollout.
The application doesn't handle SIGTERM, so the container runtime sends SIGKILL after the grace period.
Database transactions started by dying processes are left in a half-complete state, requiring manual cleanup.
The application needs to stop accepting new requests, finish in-flight work, and close connections when receiving a termination signal.
The application does not handle termination signals, failing to drain connections and complete in-flight requests before shutting down.
explanation: Graceful Shutdown Neglect is the failure to handle termination signals properly, causing in-flight requests to be dropped and resources to be left in inconsistent states.

clues: Our application takes 10 minutes to start because it must populate an in-memory cache from the database before serving traffic.
New instances cannot join the load balancer quickly, making autoscaling ineffective for sudden traffic spikes.
The startup process downloads and processes a 2GB file from S3 before the application can handle any requests.
The readiness probe doesn't pass for several minutes because the initialization work is blocking startup.
The application requires a lengthy, resource-intensive initialization phase before it can serve any traffic.
The application has a heavy preboot initialization step that must complete before it can serve requests, making startup slow and scaling sluggish.
explanation: Preboot Dependency is when an application requires a lengthy initialization phase before it can serve traffic, undermining fast scaling and deployment.

clues: The application crashes on startup if the database isn't available yet, even though it only needs the database for some features.
We have to restart services in a specific sequence after an infrastructure failure or the whole system stays down.
Service A requires Service B, which requires Service C, creating a rigid startup chain.
Container orchestration randomly starts services, so the fragile startup ordering breaks frequently.
Services should be resilient to dependencies being temporarily unavailable during startup, using retry logic and circuit breakers.
Services must be started in a strict sequence because each one immediately fails if its dependencies are not yet available.
explanation: Startup Order Dependency occurs when services require their dependencies to be available at startup, creating a rigid initialization sequence.

clues: Background job processing falls further behind during peak hours, creating a growing backlog.
The queue has thousands of pending jobs but we only have two worker processes consuming them.
We added more web server instances for HTTP traffic but forgot to scale the background workers too.
Job processing latency has grown from seconds to hours because worker capacity hasn't kept pace with demand.
The twelve-factor concurrency principle says to scale different process types independently based on their workload.
Background worker processes are not scaled to match workload demand, causing job processing backlogs while web processes are adequately scaled.
explanation: Worker Process Underscaling is failing to scale background worker processes independently to match workload demand, as recommended by the twelve-factor process model.

clues: Every time performance degrades, the solution is to request a bigger server from IT.
We've upgraded to the largest available instance type and there's nowhere left to scale.
The application uses a single process with in-memory state, making it impossible to run multiple instances.
Scaling means buying expensive hardware rather than adding commodity instances.
The twelve-factor approach recommends scaling out via the process model rather than scaling up via bigger hardware.
The application can only be scaled by adding more resources to a single machine rather than by running additional instances, hitting hardware limits.
explanation: The Vertical Scaling Trap is when an application can only scale by using more powerful hardware rather than running more instances, eventually hitting hardware ceilings.

clues: Our single server process handles HTTP requests, background jobs, and scheduled tasks all in one thread pool.
A spike in background job processing causes HTTP requests to time out because they share the same process.
We cannot scale background workers independently of web servers because they're the same process.
The twelve-factor approach recommends expressing workload diversity through different process types.
Separating web, worker, and scheduler into distinct process types would allow independent scaling and isolation.
The application bundles web serving, background processing, and scheduling into a single process type instead of separating them as distinct, independently scalable processes.
explanation: Process Type Confusion is running different types of workloads in a single process type rather than separating them for independent scaling and failure isolation.

clues: An insert storing 'N/A' in an integer column passed every local test, but production rejected it with a type error.
Developers use SQLite locally but production uses PostgreSQL, causing behavior differences.
A query that performs well locally is catastrophically slow in production due to different query planners.
The team assumed that SQL is SQL, but subtle differences between database engines cause production bugs.
Using the same database technology in development as production would catch these issues before deployment.
Developers use a different database technology locally than what runs in production, causing subtle behavioral differences that only manifest in production.
explanation: Development Database Divergence is using different database technologies in development and production, violating the twelve-factor principle of dev/prod parity.

clues: Features validated in staging frequently break when deployed to production.
Staging has half the CPU, a fraction of the data, and runs older versions of dependencies compared to production.
Bugs that appear in production cannot be reproduced in staging because the environments are too different.
The staging environment was set up two years ago and has never been updated to match production infrastructure changes.
The twelve-factor principle of dev/prod parity demands keeping environments as similar as possible.
The staging environment has drifted significantly from production in infrastructure, data, and configuration, making pre-production testing unreliable.
explanation: Staging Environment Drift is when the staging environment diverges from production in significant ways, reducing the reliability of pre-production testing.

clues: Our distributed system struggles to determine the correct ordering of concurrent updates from different nodes.
The metadata attached to each value grows linearly with the number of nodes in the cluster.
Merging concurrent updates requires understanding a partial ordering defined by pairs of node identifiers and counters.
Client requests must carry increasingly large version metadata as the cluster scales.
Each node maintains a counter per peer node, and comparing two version vectors requires element-wise comparison.
The system uses per-node logical counters to track causality across replicas, but the growing size of these version vectors creates overhead as the cluster scales.
explanation: Vector Clock Complexity refers to the growing overhead of maintaining per-node logical timestamps for causal ordering in distributed systems.

clues: Two users edited the same cart on different replicas, and one user's change silently disappeared.
The team is using a single logical timestamp per key when they need per-replica versioning to detect conflicts.
Concurrent writes are being silently overwritten because the conflict detection mechanism is insufficient.
The system needs to distinguish between 'this write happened after that one' and 'these writes were concurrent.'
The design doc claims a single Lamport counter per key is enough to flag concurrent writes as siblings.
The team is confusing version vectors, which track causality per replica per key, with simpler logical clocks that cannot fully detect concurrent updates.
explanation: Version Vector Confusion arises from misunderstanding the difference between version vectors and simpler logical clocks in multi-replica conflict detection.

clues: The team adopted a data structure for automatic conflict resolution but the results don't match business expectations.
A counter that should show total inventory is giving different values on different replicas that never converge correctly.
The automatic merge semantics work mathematically but produce results that are meaningless in the business domain.
The team chose a G-Counter when they needed a PN-Counter, causing incorrect results when items are removed.
The data type guarantees eventual consistency through mathematical properties, but the chosen type doesn't model the actual business operation.
A CRDT was applied to a problem where its automatic merge semantics produce mathematically valid but business-incorrect results due to choosing the wrong CRDT type.
explanation: CRDT Misuse occurs when a conflict-free replicated data type is applied incorrectly, producing convergent but semantically wrong results for the business domain.

clues: Our collaborative editing feature has bugs where concurrent edits sometimes produce garbled text.
The algorithm for transforming operations against each other has edge cases we keep discovering.
Character insertions at the same position by different users occasionally result in inconsistent document states.
The server must transform every incoming operation against all concurrent operations, and the order matters.
The transformation functions for different operation types create a combinatorial explosion of cases to handle correctly.
The operational transformation algorithm used for real-time collaborative editing has become unmanageably complex due to the combinatorial explosion of transformation cases.
explanation: Operational Transform Complexity refers to the difficulty of correctly implementing the OT algorithm for real-time collaboration due to its combinatorial edge cases.

clues: Search results are stale for seconds to minutes after records are updated in the primary database.
Users update their profile but the change isn't reflected in the downstream analytics system immediately.
The pipeline that streams database changes to derived systems has fallen behind during peak load.
The replication lag between the source database and the event stream consumer is growing.
The system reads the database write-ahead log to propagate changes, but consumer throughput cannot keep up with write volume.
The change data capture pipeline that streams database mutations to downstream consumers has fallen behind, causing derived data stores to serve stale data.
explanation: Change Data Capture Lag occurs when the pipeline streaming database changes to downstream systems falls behind, causing derived views to be stale.

clues: One Redis shard is at 100% CPU while the other 11 idle at 15%

One key gets so much traffic that the single node owning it becomes the bottleneck
explanation: The hot key problem occurs when a disproportionate amount of traffic targets a single key or partition, overwhelming the node responsible for it.

clues: Tiny health-check requests take 2 seconds, but only while a large report download is in flight

One slow item at the front of a FIFO queue or connection delays everything queued behind it
explanation: Head-of-line blocking occurs when a slow item at the front of a queue or connection prevents faster items behind it from being processed.

clues: We run five replicas on five servers, and all five went down in the same minute

explanation: Correlated failures occur when supposedly independent components fail together because they share an underlying dependency or failure domain.

clues: The internal PDF export service has degraded for months, and its tickets sit untriaged

explanation: An ownership vacuum occurs when a production system has no clearly assigned team responsible for maintaining, operating, and improving it.

explanation: A runaway query is a database query that consumes excessive resources, typically due to a missing index, full table scan, or unbounded result set.

clues: Lag on one Kafka consumer group grows all day and only recovers overnight

explanation: A slow consumer occurs when a message consumer processes messages slower than they are produced, leading to growing queue backlogs and latency.

clues: The consumer pod has restarted 340 times today, each time within seconds of starting

explanation: A poison pill message is a message in a queue that causes the consumer to fail repeatedly, blocking processing of all messages behind it.

clues: Right after the producer team's deploy, a downstream consumer starts failing on every new event

explanation: A schema mismatch occurs when the producer and consumer of a data format use incompatible schema versions, causing serialization or deserialization failures.

clues: Three microservices stopped serving at once, and CPU on all of them is near zero

explanation: A distributed deadlock is a deadlock that spans multiple services or nodes, where each waits on another in a cycle of synchronous remote calls.

clues: The profile page takes 1.2s to load, though each backend responds in under 20ms

explanation: Chatty microservice communication occurs when services make too many fine-grained calls to each other, causing high aggregate latency from accumulated round trips.

clues: Over the last quarter, 80% of features needed PRs in at least three services

explanation: Service boundary misalignment occurs when microservice boundaries do not match business domain boundaries, creating tight coupling and cross-service dependencies.

Splitting into many independently deployed services before team size, scale, or domain understanding justifies it
explanation: Premature microservices is the antipattern of adopting a microservice architecture before the team size, domain understanding, or scale justifies the operational complexity.

clues: A bad release reached 100% of users despite passing every automated rollout gate

explanation: A canary that doesn't catch is a deployment canary that fails to detect regressions because it monitors the wrong metrics or doesn't receive representative traffic.

clues: The cloud bill rose $2,000/month with no new launches

Cloud resources left running after the project that needed them ended, costing money and adding attack surface
explanation: Orphaned infrastructure refers to cloud resources left running after their associated project or service has been decommissioned, wasting money and creating security risk.

clues: A security scan flagged an unauthenticated route nobody on the team knew existed

explanation: Zombie endpoints are API routes that are no longer actively used but remain deployed, creating maintenance burden, security risk, and API surface bloat.

clues: A price was changed from $10 to $15, but the product page still shows $10

explanation: A stale cache serves outdated data because the cache entry has not been refreshed or invalidated after the source data changed.

clues: Coverage reports show else-branches that no environment has executed in a year

clues: On-call was paged 40 times last week, and 35 of those pages had no user impact

explanation: This antipattern is alerting on causes (CPU, memory, disk) instead of symptoms (user-facing latency, errors, availability).
